segments.t: While walking through the dining room, Chef Barinov's daughter Katya spots her childhood friend Lilya. The two women have competed fiercely since kindergarten, so when Lilya introduces her wealthy husband, Katya invents a fiancé on the spot. Let's listen to their rivalry in Russian.
Let's examine Katya and Lilya's competitive reunion line by line.
'Hello, this is my friend Katya.' Spoken Russian keeps this brief and expressive, built right around 'female friend' without extra helper words.
'We went to kindergarten together.' A multidirectional past-tense verb of motion expresses repeated round-trip attendance in childhood.
'We always argued since childhood.' Notice how Russian puts 'always' and 'childhood' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
'They accepted me into the university back then.' Here the guest anchors the thought on 'then, in that case' and finishes on 'took, arrested', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
'And I went to France.' In everyday Russian, 'france' flows straight into 'to go, to set off' without extra linking words.
'Katya, this is my husband Ernest.' the guest pairs 'husband' with 'ernest' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.
'Hello, it is very nice to meet you.' Katya uses a polite everyday Russian courtesy expression that sets the tone of the conversation right away.
'Well, and did you get married?' For a woman, Russian uses a specific verbal idiom literally meaning to step out behind a husband.
'No, but I will definitely get married soon.' In everyday Russian, 'soon' flows straight into 'I'll get out' without extra linking words.
'Our wedding is in a month.' Russians say 'by me' or 'with us' where English says 'I have' or 'we have', without needing a separate word for 'have'.
'Then let's have dinner together tomorrow evening!' Notice how Russian puts 'then, in that case' and 'together' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
'I do not know, he is very busy.' Here Katya anchors the thought on 'know' and finishes on 'busy', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.

'Great, what time are we meeting tomorrow?' In everyday Russian, 'perfectly' flows straight into 'are dating' without extra linking words. Let's listen to their dining room conversation again without interruption.
Katya's pride traps her into promising to bring her non-existent fiancé to dinner the very next evening. Listen for the feminine phrase for getting married in Russian. Until next time!
